svg.title: Three RT topologies written as tables: full mesh, hub-and-spoke, and spoke-to-spoke through the hub
svg.desc: Three panels, each with a small topology sketch and the export and import table that produces it. Full mesh: every VRF exports and imports the same route target, so every site reaches every other site directly. Hub and spoke: the hub exports its own RT and imports every spoke RT; each spoke exports its own RT and imports only the hub RT, so spokes reach each other only through the hub. Spoke to spoke through the hub: the hub additionally re-advertises, which requires the hub to import and re-export, and the note warns that this turns the hub into a transit point for spoke traffic and must be sized for it. A bottom band states the rule for building a new RT plan: derive the RT from the topology, never from the customer name, and keep one table as the authority.
svg.text: A topology drawing is an RT design; the RT table is the drawing written as data
Three topologies cover almost every request, and each is three lines of table
Full mesh
export: RT 100 on every VRF
import: RT 100 on every VRF
One RT, one line per VRF. Every site reaches
every other site directly, so N×(N−1)/2
conversations must be funded and secured.
Hub and spoke
hub
spoke1
spoke2
hub: export 100, import 101 + 102
spoke1: export 101, import 100 only
spoke2: export 102, import 100 only
The import list is where the topology lives.
Spoke to spoke via the hub
The hub must now forward traffic between
spokes, so it imports and re-exports.
hub: export 100, import 101 + 102
spokes: unchanged
The speak-to-speak path now crosses the
hub twice: size its CPU, bandwidth and
firewall policy for transit, not for a star.
Easiest change to request, hardest to
operate afterwards.
The authoritative table, one row per VRF
VRF · RD · export RT list · import RT list · domain ID (if OSPF is the PE-CE) · which topologies this site belongs to.
How RT plans go wrong: the RT is derived from the customer name, so it encodes an organisation instead of a topology. Two customers merge, or one
buys another, and the RT plan has to be rewritten across every PE. Derive the RT from the topology (mesh, hub, shared service) and the same
change becomes one import line. This is the single cheapest decision in an L3VPN design, and the one most often made by accident.
Keep the table in version control. When it lives in a spreadsheet on someone's laptop, the network is already undocumented.
